Solution 1 (Binary Search)
Clearly, trying to bruteforce over all possible values of $x$ or $y$ is too slow, because the bounds are $1 \leq l_1 \leq r_1 \leq 10^9$.

This is because $2^{32} \gt 10^9$, so there cannot possibly be any solutions for $n \gt 32$ for any $k$.

Solution 2 (Intervals)
Note that we do not need to care about more than $32$ different values of $k^n$, because obviously $k^{32} \ge 2^{32} \gt 10^9$.

Formally, this condition can be cleared out as:
$l_2 \le x k^n \le r_2$
$\frac{l_2}{k^n} \le x \le \frac{r_2}{k^n}$
Because $x$ is an integer, $\left \lceil {\frac{l_2}{k^n}} \right \rceil \le x \le \left \lfloor {\frac{r_2}{k^n}} \right \rfloor$
Thus, when we intersect the two intervals, we get the following interval at last.
$\max \left({l_1,\left \lceil {\frac{l_2}{k^n}} \right \rceil}\right) \le x \le \min \left({r_1,\left \lfloor {\frac{r_2}{k^n}} \right \rfloor}\right)$
Compute the size of this interval for all $k^n$ (at most $32$ values) and the answer can be found.

Dealing with big integers can be helpful in avoiding this, but it may make your solution slow.

Solution
Consider a particular query.

We can compute and store the divisors of all integers $2\leq a_i\leq 10^5$ in $O(A\log A)$ time in a vector of vectors where $divisor[a_i]$ contains all divisors of $a_i$ as follows: for all $2\leq i\leq A$, we push $i$ into $divisors[j]$ for all multiples $j$ of $i$. (The runtime follows from the fact that there are $\lfloor\frac{A}{i}\rfloor$ multiples of $i$ which are at most $A$, so across all $i$, we have at most $\frac{A}{1} + \frac{A}{2} + \cdots + \frac{A}{A} = A(\frac{1}{1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{A}) = AH(A) = O(A\log A)$ computations).

Hint 2
Can we use this to bound the number of times $k$ changes?
Answer
For each divisor $d$ of $k$, $k$ can only change once, because after the first iteration with $a[i] = d$, $k$ is no longer divisible by $d$.

Thus, the number of times $k$ changes is bounded by the number of divisors of $k$.

This allows us to bound the number of times $k$ changes by $d(k)$, where $d(k)$ is the number of divisors of $k$.

Note that the divisors of $d(k)$ can be found in $O(\sqrt{k})$ time by checking if $a$ divides $k$ for every $a$ from $2$ to $\sqrt{k}$, and if so, $a$ and $\frac{k}{a}$ are both divisors of $k$.

Furthermore, at the scale constrained by the problem bounds, $d(k)$ is around $O(\sqrt[3]{k})$, so we only have to update $k$ at most $O(\sqrt[3]{k})$ times.

Now, we would like to find the first time each divisor of $k$ appears in $a[l], \dots, a[r]$.

This allows us to solve the problem in $O(n\log{n})$ preprocessing time and $O(\sqrt{k} + d(k)\log{n})$ time per query.

There are a few ways to optimize the runtime further, if your implementation is too slow.

For a time $t$, we can calculate $c_t$ using prefix sums as it is the sum of $c_{t-1}$ and the number of people that sit down at time $t$.

At least $a_i$ people have already sat down strictly before time $t$.

At least one of their neighbors (person $i-1$ or $i+1$, if they exist) has already sat down strictly before time $t$.

A person is of this type if the earliest time one of their neighbours sat down is exactly $1$ less than the time they sat down.

A person is of this type if the time they sit down is at least $2$ greater than the earliest time one of their neighbours sat down.

Since they did not sit down at time $t-1$, their $a_i$ must be greater than $c_{t-2}$.

This fails if and only if $m$ is a multiple of $k$, because we see that horizontally adjacent elements differ by $1\pmod k$ and vertically adjacent elements differ by $m\pmod k$.

The definition essentially asks for the largest index $k$ such that the $\gcd$ of the first $k$ elements is strictly greater than the $\gcd$ of the first $k+1$.

A useful observation is that scaling the entire array (multiplying or dividing every element by the same integer) does not affect where this drop occurs; each $\gcd$ value is just scaled accordingly.

This allows us to 'normalize' the problem: divide each $a_i$ by the $\gcd$ of the whole array.

After this, the $\gcd$ of the full array becomes $1$, and the question reduces to:
What is the last index where the prefix GCD is still greater than $1$?
Now, note that $\gcd \gt 1$ for a prefix means there exists some integer $d \gt 1$ that divides every element in that prefix.

Maintain a frequency array $\text{div}$, where $\text{div}[d]$ stores how many elements seen so far are divisible by $d$.

Extending to Prefixes
The problem, however, doesn’t just ask for $f(a)$ of the entire array.

Fortunately, the divisor-counting approach extends naturally: as we iterate through the array from left to right, we update the divisor frequencies for each new element and recompute the maximum.

For the addition operation, acknowledge that if we add an element to an array, it only changes the $\operatorname{mex}$ of the array if the element is equal to the $\operatorname{mex}$, in which case the $\operatorname{mex}$ of the array will be changed to the $\operatorname{secondMex}$ of the array, or the second smallest positive integer that is not present in the array.

title: The 67th Integer Problem - Common Mistakes
summary: A common mistake was to output $y=x+1$, which fails because $68$ is greater than $67$, therefore not a valid output.
